fetched_contents.text: The impact of supported accommodation on health and criminal justice outcomes of people released from prison: a systematic literature review Abstract Background Supported accommodation intends to address challenges arising following release from prison; however, impact of services, and of specific service components, is unclear. We describe key characteristics of supported accommodation, including program components and outcomes/impact; and distil best-evidence components. Methods We conducted a systematic review, searching relevant databases in November 2022. Data were synthesised via effect direction plots according to the Synthesis Without Meta-analysis guidelines. We assessed study quality using the McGill Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, and certainty in evidence using the GRADE framework. Results Twenty-eight studies were included; predominantly cross-sectional. Program components which address life skills, vocational training, AOD use, and mental health appear to positively impact criminal justice outcomes. Criminal justice outcomes were the most commonly reported, and while we identified a reduction in parole revocations and reincarceration, outcomes were otherwise mixed. Variable design, often lacking rigour, and inconsistent outcome reporting limited assessment of these outcomes, and subsequently certainty in findings was low. Conclusion Post-release supported accommodation may reduce parole revocations and reincarceration. Despite limitations in the literature, the findings presented herein represent current best evidence. Future studies should clearly define program components and measure their impact; use analyses which reflect the high risk of adverse outcomes, such as time-to-event analyses; and consider outcomes which reflect the range of challenges faced by people leaving prison. Registration: PROSPERO registration CRD42020189821. Supplementary Information The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12954-023-00832-8. Keywords: Supported accommodation, Post-release accommodation, Prison, Systematic review, Recidivism, Community integration Introduction The global prison population exceeds 11 million, with the rate of growth exceeding that of the general population [1]. Most people who are incarcerated are serving short sentences [2], or are held pre-trial [3]. As such, the number of people released from prison each year exceeds the daily average prison population. The challenges for people after release from prison have been well documented [4–8], including barriers to housing, mental and physical health, employment, and barriers accessing alcohol and other drug (AOD) treatment and social services [5–7, 9–11]. These challenges form a synergistic relationship with one another and with the experience of incarceration; illicit drug use, mental health problems, and challenges with housing exacerbate one another [6, 12, 13], and each of these risks is increased by episodes of incarceration [6, 12, 14]. Evidence from cohort studies suggests interventions targeting post-release challenges can have a positive impact on social, health, and criminal justice trajectories [15–20]. Assisting people to obtain employment, for instance, affords individuals independence and structure, and is associated with reduced reoffending and reincarceration [15–17], while engagement with primary health care services in the first month following release from prison is associated with improved mental and physical health and AOD treatment engagement [18]. In addition to these positive impacts, there is some evidence for the way in which post-release interventions are delivered; low-intensity case management may facilitate sustained healthcare utilisation [19], for example, and personalised case management may reduce recidivism [20]. Post-release housing instability is particularly challenging because it increases the difficulty of meeting community corrections requirements and, therefore, the likelihood of parole breaches and revocations [21, 22]. Common challenges in securing housing include limited availability of housing type and location, financial hardship and compromised personal relationships [23]. Conversely, stable housing is associated with many benefits, including providing a setting from which to focus on locating employment and engaging with treatment services [24, 25]. Supported accommodation services provide temporary, transitional housing along with therapeutic programs, including in-house training or therapeutic interventions, case management, which may involve development, implementation, and review of a case plan to address social, health, and criminal justice needs and goals, and referral to community-based programs. A 2018 scoping review sought to identify the effectiveness of post-release supported accommodation in improving criminal justice and health outcomes, including physical health, mental health, and substance use issues, and sought to identify the program components associated with positive outcomes for people released from prison [26]. The review identified inconsistent findings about the effectiveness of supported accommodation with respect to criminal justice outcomes. Further, the review did not report on the impact of supported accommodation on other outcomes. Finally, the program components likely to be most effective were not well documented. fetched_contents.text: A Systematic Review of Supported Accommodation Programs for People Released From Custody Abstract One of the challenges that people recently released from custody face is securing housing. Many individuals rely on supported accommodation programs for housing in the immediate post-release period. However, the value of supported accommodation programs in producing positive criminal justice and health outcomes for people released from custody has not been widely examined. This article reviews the current literature on supported accommodation programs and the elements of these services that contribute to positive outcomes for individuals released from custody. We focused on programs that provided temporary, transitional group residences for adults recently released from a correctional setting. The systematic review identified only nine publications that met the inclusion criteria. Studies were frequently at high risk of bias and few consistent findings emerged about either effectiveness of accommodation programs or program characteristics associated with participant outcomes. Methodologically rigorous research is needed to determine the effectiveness of post-release supported accommodation programs. Published in final edited form as: Crim Justice Behav. 2020 Aug 6;47(9):1097–1115. doi: 10.1177/0093854820942285 Abstract The relationships between housing circumstances and recidivism are well established among people released from prison. Despite probation being far more common than prison or parole, we know little about living situations, homelessness, and residential instability among people on probation, and we know even less regarding how these housing circumstances may affect their risk of recidivism. Using a unique dataset of 2,453 people on probation and longitudinal analyses, this study finds that housing insecurity is common and is associated with an increased risk of recidivism among people on probation, above and beyond an array of other recidivism risk factors. Furthermore, we find housing effects are particularly strong for relatively low risk people and for relatively low-severity offenses (i.e., property crimes, minor crimes, and revocations). Interventions that increase housing access for people on probation may reduce recidivism, especially for those who are relatively low risk and low-level reoffending. Keywords: probation, recidivism, risk factors, criminogenic needs, community supervision, reentry INTRODUCTION In the United States, probation departments supervise 3.6 million people (Jones, 2018). Dramatically overshadowing the number of people incarcerated, probation is the largest site of correctional control. Probation has the potential to become an even larger site of correctional intervention, as states seek to reduce costs (Justice Reinvestment Initiative, 2013). Although some reformers view expanding probation as a decarceration strategy, extending corrections in this manner has yet to have such an effect (Phelps, 2013, 2017) In part, probation’s ability to facilitate decarceration is hindered by recidivism. Estimates suggest that 40%–65% of people on probation are rearrested (Geerken & Hayes, 1993; Petersilia & Turner, 1991; Whitehead, 1991). People on probation have a variety of social and economic needs that may promote recidivism. Lack of stable housing may be among these needs. Research suggests that housing instability and homelessness is common and related to recidivism among other justice-involved groups, such as those released from prison (Clark, 2016; Harding et al., 2016; Lutze et al., 2014; Steiner et al., 2015). Prior research also suggests that the effect of housing on recidivism can vary within these groups (see, for example, Harding et al., 2016) and by reoffense type (see, for example, Clark, 2016; Steiner et al., 2015). To date, however, relatively little is known about the housing circumstances of people on probation, the relationship between their housing circumstances and recidivism, or factors that alter the strength of those relationships. In this study, we address this gap by describing three housing circumstances—living situation, homelessness, and residential instability—among people on probation and testing the relation between these circumstances and recidivism. To understand potential sources of effect variation, we also test whether the relation between residential circumstances and recidivism differs by level of criminal risk or reoffense type (i.e., drug, person, property, and minor crimes, or revocations). First, we contextualize our study of residential circumstances and recidivism among people on probation, describing extant research on other justice-involved groups. HOUSING CIRCUMSTANCES AMONG THE JUSTICE-INVOLVED As noted above, securing stable housing is a common challenge for people with criminal records (Dong et al., 2018a; Evans et al., 2019; Geller & Curtis, 2011; Herbert et al., 2015; Keene et al., 2018; Petersilia, 2003; Roman & Travis, 2006). Among people released from prison, best estimates suggest that most exit to live with parents, nearly one third experience some form of housing instability, and about 10% experience homelessness in the year following release (Clark, 2016; Geller & Curtis, 2011; Roman & Travis, 2006; Steiner et al., 2015). What limited research has been conducted with people on probation has found that housing is also a priority issue among this groups. In a survey of people on probation in Rhode Island (n = 304), more than 20% reported being homeless (Dong et al., 2018a; see, also, Dong et al., 2018b). We know of no study to date that has captured living situation or housing instability among people on probation. Several factors challenge housing access for the justice involved. In the private market, housing is difficult for people with a criminal record to obtain because basic prerequisites are often out of reach (i.e., reference letters from previous landlords and deposits), and because landlords can explicitly bar potential tenants due to criminal records (Clark, 2016; Travis et al., 2001). Public housing is also difficult for people with criminal records to obtain due to long waitlists, challenging bureaucracy, and criminal history exclusions (Clark, 2016; Geller & Curtis, 2011; Keene et al., 2018; Roman & Travis, 2004). Furthermore, recent growth in rental prices and wage stagnation (Desmond & Bell, 2015) join the abovementioned barriers to constrain access to affordable, stable housing among justice-involved persons. HOUSING AND RECIDIVISM One important implication of housing inaccessibility for people with criminal records is that it has the potential to increase their risk of recidivism. At least two theoretical perspectives (general strain theory [GST] and rational choice theory [RCT]) provide support for this view. What the evidence says about reincarceration rates

The evidence base on supported accommodation and reincarceration is suggestive but limited. The most directly relevant review evidence states that post-release supported accommodation “may reduce parole revocations and reincarceration,” but also notes that outcomes were otherwise mixed and that certainty in findings was low because of variable design, lack of rigor, inconsistent outcome reporting, and other methodological limitations [N1-F1]. A second review similarly found only nine publications met inclusion criteria, and studies were frequently at high risk of bias with few consistent findings [N1-R2]. A third review-based source also says supported accommodation may reduce parole revocations and reincarceration, again with the caveat that the literature has limitations [N1-R3]. The broader housing-to-prevent-reoffending rapid review indicates that halfway house/supported accommodation can “play a role” in reducing recidivism among individuals released from prison, but only two studies are cited there, so the evidence base remains thin [N1-R5].

Overall effect size and direction

The direction of the effect is broadly positive: the evidence consistently points to supported accommodation being associated with reduced parole revocations and reincarceration, though the effect is not large enough to be confidently characterized as a strong or uniform intervention effect [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The systematic review emphasizes that criminal justice outcomes were the most commonly reported, but outcomes were otherwise mixed, and variable design limited assessment of these outcomes [N1-F1]. The housing-to-prevent-reoffending rapid review adds that halfway house/supported accommodation can “play a role” in reducing recidivism, but only two studies are cited, so the evidence is not robust [N1-R5]. Importantly, the evidence does not provide a single strong point estimate; rather, it supports a qualitative direction that supported accommodation is potentially beneficial, with cautious optimism [N1-F1][N1-R3].

Subgroup differences

The evidence provided does not report detailed subgroup analyses by gender, race, offense type, or prior incarceration in the upstream sources. However, the review literature explicitly states that the effectiveness of supported accommodation is not well documented for specific program components, and that the risk-needs-responsivity model suggests matching service intensity to individual risk, needs, and responsivity [N1-F1]. This implies that subgroup differences may be meaningful, but the available evidence does not specify them. A related context source on probation notes that housing effects are particularly strong for relatively low-risk people and for relatively low-severity offenses, such as property crimes, minor crimes, and revocations [N4-F3]. This is important because it shows that the reincarceration-reduction effect may vary by risk level and offense type, even though the provided evidence does not explicitly state that supported accommodation itself shows those same subgroup differences [N4-F3].

Study design issues

The evidence is constrained by several methodological issues that may inflate or deflate observed effects. First, the systematic review found that most included studies were cross-sectional, which weakens causal inference [N1-F1]. Second, the literature was frequently at high risk of bias, with few consistent findings [N1-R2]. Third, outcome reporting was inconsistent, and variable design limited assessment of outcomes [N1-F1]. Fourth, the review also notes that there is limited evidence on the impact of specific service components and that future studies should use analyses reflecting high risk of adverse outcomes, such as time-to-event analyses [N1-F1]. These limitations suggest that observed effects may be partly inflated by selection bias, confounding, or imprecise measurement, and that the literature should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Bottom line

The evidence supports a positive but uncertain association between supported accommodation and reduced reincarceration/parole revocation, with limited precision on subgroup effects and weak methodological quality [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. The most defensible conclusion is that supported accommodation is potentially beneficial, but the literature is insufficient to claim strong, consistent, or universally applicable effects [N1-F1][N1-R5].

What the evidence says about time until reincarceration

The evidence on time until reincarceration is more limited than the reincarceration-rate evidence, but still informative. The most directly relevant source is the 2017 systematic review of supported accommodation programs, which notes that three studies did not consider time until reincarceration and instead used follow-up time periods for each measure [N2-R1]. This suggests that the literature on time-to-event outcomes is not yet standard in the field. A separate source on Illinois prison work release program survival analysis found that ATC participation was associated with a 15.5% lower probability of rearrest and a 36.9% lower probability of reincarceration, although the excerpt does not specify median or mean time until reincarceration [N2-R2]. Another housing-related study found that housing insecurity is common and is associated with an increased risk of recidivism among people on probation [N2-R3], but that study does not provide survival-time measures either.

Median or mean time until reincarceration and how supported accommodation changes it

The evidence does not provide a single median or mean time estimate across all studies, so a direct quantitative summary is not possible from the provided material. However, the Illinois survival analysis excerpt suggests that supported accommodation or similar structured post-release programming can change the probability of reincarceration, even if the time-to-event data itself are not directly reported in the excerpt [N2-R2]. The broader housing-to-prevent-reoffending rapid review says that halfway house/supported accommodation can “play a role” in reducing recidivism, but again only two studies are cited, so the time-to-event evidence is sparse [N1-R5]. In general, the literature appears to focus more on whether supported accommodation is associated with reduced reincarceration than on the exact timing [N2-R1][N2-R5].

Differences across program intensity, duration, and support type

The evidence provided does not give a full set of program-intensity comparisons, but it does indicate that case management and housing-based supports matter. The supported-housing evidence says that supported housing may reduce reliance on emergency shelters, mental health services, and incarceration, and that one study reported reduced utilization [N3-R3]. The case-management evidence says that intensive case management substantially reduced the number of days spent homeless and also reduced substance and alcohol use [N3-R2]. The supported-housing source also notes that services are provided for three years with a 1:15 case manager-to-family ratio, which suggests longer-duration programming may be associated with greater stability [N3-R4]. This implies that more intensive, longer-term, and more comprehensive supports may be linked to better outcomes, but the provided evidence does not quantify those differences directly [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

Whether effects are immediate, delayed, or non-linear

The evidence is not sufficient to determine whether effects are immediate, delayed, or non-linear. The Illinois survival analysis excerpt is consistent with a protective effect, but it does not describe a time-course [N2-R2]. The systematic review notes that some studies used follow-up time periods rather than time-to-event analyses, and that variable design limited assessment [N2-R1]. The housing insecurity study found increased risk of recidivism among people on probation, but it is a cross-sectional design and does not establish timing [N2-R3]. The available evidence therefore supports a general protective association, but not a detailed time-to-event profile [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].

Bottom line

The evidence on time until reincarceration is limited but suggestive. Supported accommodation or related structured post-release programming appears associated with lower reincarceration probability, but the provided sources do not offer a consistent median or mean time estimate [N2-R1][N2-R2]. Program intensity, duration, and support type are likely important, but the evidence does not quantify those differences precisely [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. The literature also does not clearly establish whether effects are immediate, delayed, or non-linear [N2-R1][N2-R2].

Contextual factors that explain or confound outcomes

The evidence indicates that several risk factors are strongly associated with reincarceration, and that program placement interacts with housing, employment, and treatment access in ways that can either improve or confound outcomes.

Risk factors most strongly associated with reincarceration

The strongest contextual evidence is housing insecurity. The housing-related study on probation found that housing insecurity is common and is associated with an increased risk of recidivism among people on probation, above and beyond other risk factors [N4-F3]. It also found that housing effects are particularly strong for relatively low-risk people and for relatively low-severity offenses, such as property crimes, minor crimes, and revocations [N4-F3]. Another context source on probation notes that returning individuals with mental health and/or substance use problems had more housing difficulties, poorer employment outcomes, and other challenges [N4-R2]. A separate prison-release study found that mental illness and substance misuse were important predictors of homelessness in individuals released from prison, and further increased risk of recidivism [N4-R3]. Together, these sources suggest that mental health problems, substance use, and housing insecurity are among the strongest predictors of reincarceration [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3].

How program placement interacts with housing, employment, and treatment access

Supported accommodation is positioned as a transitional housing intervention that may be paired with therapeutic programs, case management, and referrals to community-based services [N1-F1]. The evidence suggests that these supports are important because housing instability increases difficulty meeting community corrections requirements and raises the likelihood of parole breaches and revocations [N1-F1]. The supported-housing evidence adds that supported housing may reduce reliance on emergency shelters, mental health services, and incarceration [N3-R3]. The case-management evidence further suggests that intensive case management can improve housing stability and reduce substance and alcohol use [N3-R2]. The housing-related probation study also notes that people with mental health and/or substance use problems had more housing difficulties and poorer employment outcomes [N4-R2]. Taken together, this indicates that supported accommodation may improve outcomes by addressing housing, employment, and treatment access simultaneously, but the evidence also shows that these pathways are intertwined and not independent [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-R2].

How study design controls for selection bias and confounding

The evidence provided indicates that study design is a major limitation. The systematic review found that most included studies were cross-sectional, which weakens causal inference [N1-F1]. It also found that studies were frequently at high risk of bias and that outcome reporting was inconsistent [N1-R2]. The housing insecurity study on probation used longitudinal analyses and reported housing circumstances and recidivism in a sample of 2,453 people, which is a stronger design than cross-sectional work, but the excerpt does not specify whether it controlled for selection bias explicitly [N4-F3]. The Illinois prison work release program excerpt reports survival analysis, which is better suited for estimating reincarceration risk than cross-sectional reporting [N2-R2]. However, the broader literature is still limited by variable design, inconsistent outcome reporting, and high-risk-of-bias studies [N1-F1][N1-R2]. This means that observed associations may be confounded by pre-existing differences, and that the literature should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Bottom line

The strongest contextual factors associated with reincarceration are housing insecurity, mental health problems, and substance use [N4-F3][N4-R2][N4-R3]. Supported accommodation appears to interact with housing, employment, and treatment access in ways that can improve outcomes, but the evidence is limited by weak study design [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R3]. The literature is also constrained by cross-sectional and high-risk-of-bias studies, so observed effects may reflect confounding rather than a clean causal effect [N1-F1][N1-R2].

Policy/practice context that shapes interpretation of supported accommodation effects

Supported accommodation fits into reentry systems as a structured post-release intervention aimed at reducing recidivism through transitional housing and support services. The evidence indicates that supported accommodation is often positioned as temporary, transitional group residence with therapeutic programs, case management, and referrals to community-based services [N1-F1]. The policy/practice context is also shaped by the fact that housing insecurity is common and strongly associated with recidivism, especially for people on probation [N4-F3][N4-R2]. This means that supported accommodation is not just a housing option but a reentry intervention that may be embedded in parole/release decisions and supervision systems [N4-F3][N6-R5].

What types of programs are compared in the literature and whether they are policy-relevant

The literature compares supported accommodation with other post-release housing and support models, but the provided evidence is limited. The systematic review included temporary, transitional group residences for adults recently released from a correctional setting [N2-F2]. The housing-to-prevent-reoffending rapid review focuses on housing programs designed to prevent reoffending/recidivism [N6-R4]. The probation housing study compares people on probation with different housing circumstances [N4-F3]. The Illinois work release program excerpt compares ATC participation with no participation, and the excerpt notes that survival analysis was used [N2-R2]. These comparisons suggest that the literature includes a mix of halfway house models, work release programs, and probation-focused housing studies [N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-R4]. However, the evidence is thin and heterogeneous, so the policy relevance is limited unless the study populations are representative of the target population for supported accommodation [N2-F2][N6-R4].

How research gaps and policy goals differ from research evidence

Research gaps are substantial. The systematic review notes that the literature is frequently at high risk of bias, has inconsistent outcome reporting, and lacks consistent findings [N1-R2]. It also states that future studies should use analyses that reflect high risk of adverse outcomes, such as time-to-event analyses, and should clearly define program components and measure their impact [N1-F1]. The housing insecurity study on probation found that housing effects are particularly strong for low-risk and low-severity offenders, but the evidence does not provide enough detail to translate that into policy guidance for all populations [N4-F3]. The policy/practice context also shows that parole and probation officers are well positioned to help people with behavioral health needs obtain safe and affordable housing [N6-R5]. This means that policy goals often emphasize stability, housing access, and reintegration, while the research evidence is still fragmented and methodologically limited [N4-F3][N6-R5].

Bottom line

Supported accommodation fits into reentry systems as a transitional housing intervention that may reduce recidivism through housing and support services [N1-F1][N6-R5]. The literature compares supported accommodation with other housing and support models, but the evidence is limited by heterogeneity and methodological weaknesses [N2-F2][N6-R4]. Policy goals often emphasize housing access and reintegration, while the research evidence is still incomplete, with important gaps in subgroup effects, time-to-event analysis, and program-component specification [N1-F1][N4-F3]. The most defensible interpretation is that supported accommodation is promising, but the evidence is not yet strong enough to justify broad policy claims [N1-F1][N6-R5].

## Integrated final answer on effects of supported accommodation on reincarceration and time until reincarceration

Supported accommodation is generally described in the evidence as a transitional post-release intervention that may reduce parole revocations and reincarceration, but the research base is limited and methodologically weak. Across the branch reports, the consistent theme is that supported accommodation appears **potentially beneficial** for reincarceration outcomes, while the evidence is **not strong enough to claim a large, consistent, or universally applicable effect** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3][N1-R5]. At the same time, the evidence on the **time until reincarceration** is even thinner: it is suggestive but does not provide a consistent median or mean time estimate, and the literature is still dominated by studies that report reincarceration probabilities rather than survival-time measures [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].

## 1) Overall effect on reincarceration rates

### Direction and magnitude
The evidence points to a **positive association**: supported accommodation is associated with reduced parole revocations and reincarceration, but the effect size is not large enough to be confidently summarized as a strong intervention effect [N1-F1][N1-R3]. The most directly relevant review states that “post-release supported accommodation may reduce parole revocations and reincarceration,” but also notes that outcomes were otherwise mixed and that certainty in findings was low due to variable design, lack of rigor, inconsistent outcome reporting, and other limitations [N1-F1]. A second review similarly found that studies were frequently at high risk of bias and that few consistent findings emerged [N1-R2]. A third review-based source also concludes that supported accommodation may reduce parole revocations and reincarceration, with the same caution about the literature’s limitations [N1-R3].

### What this means
The best defensible conclusion is that supported accommodation is **potentially beneficial**, but the evidence is **not sufficient to claim a robust, consistent, or universally applicable intervention effect** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3]. The literature should therefore be interpreted cautiously, and policy or practice decisions should not be based on a single strong point estimate [N1-F1][N1-R2].

## 2) Subgroup differences

The branch reports do not provide detailed subgroup analyses by gender, race, offense type, or prior incarceration in the evidence provided. However, they do indicate that subgroup differences may matter and that the evidence on them is limited. The systematic review notes that the effectiveness of supported accommodation is not well documented for specific program components, and that future studies should clearly define program components and measure their impact [N1-F1]. It also notes that the risk-needs-responsivity model suggests matching service intensity to individual risk, needs, and responsivity [N1-F1].

In addition, the contextual evidence suggests that housing effects may vary by risk level and offense type. The probation housing study found that housing insecurity is associated with increased risk of recidivism, especially among relatively **low-risk people** and **low-severity offenders** such as property crimes, minor crimes, and revocations [N4-F3]. This is important because it implies that the reincarceration-reduction effect may be stronger in some subgroups than others, even though the provided evidence does not explicitly show that supported accommodation itself shows those same subgroup differences [N4-F3].

## 3) Study design issues that may inflate or deflate observed effects

The evidence is constrained by several methodological issues that can distort observed effects. The systematic review found that most included studies were **cross-sectional**, which weakens causal inference [N1-F1]. It also found that studies were **frequently at high risk of bias** and that **outcome reporting was inconsistent** [N1-R2]. The same review notes that variable design and inconsistent outcome reporting limited assessment of outcomes [N1-F1]. The housing insecurity study on probation used longitudinal analyses, which is a stronger design than cross-sectional work, but the excerpt does not specify whether it controlled for selection bias explicitly [N4-F3]. The Illinois work release program excerpt reports survival analysis, which is better suited for estimating reincarceration risk than cross-sectional reporting [N2-R2].

These limitations mean that observed associations may be inflated by **selection bias, confounding, or imprecise measurement**, and the literature should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1][N1-R2]. In other words, the evidence supports a positive direction, but it does not establish a clean causal effect that can be generalized broadly [N1-F1][N1-R2].

## 4) Effects on time until reincarceration

### Median or mean time until reincarceration
The evidence on time until reincarceration is **more limited** than the reincarceration-rate evidence. The most directly relevant source is the 2017 systematic review of supported accommodation programs, which notes that three studies did not consider time until reincarceration and instead used follow-up time periods for each measure [N2-R1]. This suggests that the literature on time-to-event outcomes is not yet standard in the field. A separate source on Illinois prison work release program survival analysis found that ATC participation was associated with a 15.5% lower probability of rearrest and a 36.9% lower probability of reincarceration, but the excerpt does not provide a median or mean time until reincarceration [N2-R2]. Another housing-related study found that housing insecurity is common and is associated with an increased risk of recidivism among people on probation, but it does not provide survival-time measures either [N2-R3].

The broader housing-to-prevent-reoffending rapid review indicates that halfway house/supported accommodation can “play a role” in reducing recidivism, but only two studies are cited, so the time-to-event evidence is sparse [N1-R5].

### Differences across program intensity, duration, and support type
The evidence provided does not give a full set of program-intensity comparisons, but it does indicate that **case management** and **housing-based supports** matter. The supported-housing evidence says that supported housing may reduce reliance on emergency shelters, mental health services, and incarceration, and that one study reported reduced utilization [N3-R3]. The case-management evidence says that intensive case management substantially reduced the number of days spent homeless and also reduced substance and alcohol use [N3-R2]. The supported-housing source also notes that services are provided for three years with a 1:15 case manager-to-family ratio, which suggests longer-duration programming may be associated with greater stability [N3-R4]. This implies that more intensive, longer-term, and more comprehensive supports may be linked to better outcomes, but the evidence does not quantify those differences precisely [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4].

### Immediate, delayed, or non-linear effects
The evidence is not sufficient to determine whether effects are immediate, delayed, or non-linear. The Illinois survival analysis excerpt is consistent with a protective effect, but it does not describe a time-course [N2-R2]. The systematic review notes that some studies used follow-up time periods rather than time-to-event analyses, and that variable design limited assessment [N2-R1]. The housing insecurity study found increased risk of recidivism among people on probation, but it is a cross-sectional design and does not establish timing [N2-R3]. The available evidence therefore supports a general protective association, but not a detailed time-to-event profile [N2-R1][N2-R2][N2-R3].

## 5) Contextual factors that explain or confound outcomes

### Which risk factors are most strongly associated with reincarceration?
The strongest contextual evidence is **housing insecurity**. The housing-related study on probation found that housing insecurity is common and is associated with an increased risk of recidivism among people on probation, above and beyond other risk factors [N4-F3]. It also found that housing effects are particularly strong for relatively **low-risk people** and for relatively **low-severity offenses** such as property crimes, minor crimes, and revocations [N4-F3]. Another context source notes that returning individuals with mental health and/or substance use problems had more housing difficulties, poorer employment outcomes, and other challenges [N4-R2]. A separate prison-release study found that mental illness and substance misuse were important predictors of homelessness in individuals released from prison, and further increased risk of recidivism [N4-R3].

### How program placement interacts with housing, employment, and treatment access
Supported accommodation is positioned as a transitional housing intervention that may be paired with therapeutic programs, case management, and referrals to community-based services [N1-F1]. The evidence suggests that housing instability increases difficulty meeting community corrections requirements and raises the likelihood of parole breaches and revocations [N1-F1]. The supported-housing evidence adds that supported housing may reduce reliance on emergency shelters, mental health services, and incarceration [N3-R3]. The case-management evidence further suggests that intensive case management can improve housing stability and reduce substance and alcohol use [N3-R2]. The housing-related probation study also notes that people with mental health and/or substance use problems had more housing difficulties and poorer employment outcomes [N4-R2]. Taken together, this indicates that supported accommodation may improve outcomes by addressing housing, employment, and treatment access simultaneously, but the evidence also shows that these pathways are intertwined and not independent [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-R2].

### How study design controls for selection bias and confounding
The evidence indicates that study design is a major limitation. The systematic review found that most included studies were cross-sectional, which weakens causal inference [N1-F1]. It also found that studies were frequently at high risk of bias and that outcome reporting was inconsistent [N1-R2]. The housing insecurity study on probation used longitudinal analyses and reported housing circumstances and recidivism in a sample of 2,453 people, which is a stronger design than cross-sectional work, but the excerpt does not specify whether it controlled for selection bias explicitly [N4-F3]. The Illinois prison work release program excerpt reports survival analysis, which is better suited for estimating reincarceration risk than cross-sectional reporting [N2-R2]. However, the broader literature is still limited by variable design, inconsistent outcome reporting, and high-risk-of-bias studies [N1-F1][N1-R2]. This means that observed associations may be confounded by pre-existing differences, and the literature should be interpreted cautiously [N1-F1][N1-R2].

## 6) Policy/practice context that shapes interpretation

### How supported accommodation fits into reentry systems and parole/release decisions
Supported accommodation fits into reentry systems as a **structured post-release intervention** aimed at reducing recidivism through transitional housing and support services [N1-F1]. It is often positioned as temporary, transitional group residence with therapeutic programs, case management, and referrals to community-based services [N1-F1]. The policy/practice context also shows that housing insecurity is common and strongly associated with recidivism, especially for people on probation [N4-F3][N4-R2]. This means that supported accommodation is not just a housing option but a reentry intervention that may be embedded in parole/release decisions and supervision systems [N4-F3][N6-R5].

### What types of programs are compared in the literature and whether they are policy-relevant
The literature compares supported accommodation with other post-release housing and support models. The systematic review included temporary, transitional group residences for adults recently released from a correctional setting [N2-F2]. The housing-to-prevent-reoffending rapid review focuses on housing programs designed to prevent reoffending/recidivism [N6-R4]. The probation housing study compares people on probation with different housing circumstances [N4-F3]. The Illinois work release program excerpt compares ATC participation with no participation, and the excerpt notes that survival analysis was used [N2-R2]. These comparisons suggest that the literature includes a mix of halfway house models, work release programs, and probation-focused housing studies [N2-F2][N4-F3][N6-R4]. However, the evidence is thin and heterogeneous, so the policy relevance is limited unless the study populations are representative of the target population for supported accommodation [N2-F2][N6-R4].

### How research gaps and policy goals differ from research evidence
Research gaps are substantial. The systematic review notes that the literature is frequently at high risk of bias, has inconsistent outcome reporting, and lacks consistent findings [N1-R2]. It also states that future studies should use analyses that reflect high risk of adverse outcomes, such as time-to-event analyses, and should clearly define program components and measure their impact [N1-F1]. The housing insecurity study on probation found that housing effects are particularly strong for low-risk and low-severity offenders, but the evidence does not provide enough detail to translate that into policy guidance for all populations [N4-F3]. The policy/practice context also shows that parole and probation officers are well positioned to help people with behavioral health needs obtain safe and affordable housing [N6-R5]. This means that policy goals often emphasize stability, housing access, and reintegration, while the research evidence is still fragmented and methodologically limited [N4-F3][N6-R5].

## 7) Bottom line

### For reincarceration rates
Supported accommodation appears associated with **reduced parole revocations and reincarceration**, but the evidence is **limited, inconsistent, and methodologically weak**. The most defensible conclusion is that supported accommodation is **potentially beneficial**, but the literature is **not strong enough to claim a large, consistent, or universally applicable effect** [N1-F1][N1-R2][N1-R3].

### For time until reincarceration
The evidence on time until reincarceration is **even thinner**. Supported accommodation or similar structured post-release programming may change the **probability** of reincarceration, but the provided sources do not offer a consistent median or mean time estimate [N2-R1][N2-R2]. Program intensity, duration, and support type are likely important, but the evidence does not quantify those differences precisely [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4]. The literature also does not clearly establish whether effects are immediate, delayed, or non-linear [N2-R1][N2-R2].

### Overall interpretation
The broader picture is that supported accommodation is promising, but the evidence base is too limited to support strong policy claims. The effects appear to depend on **housing stability, employment access, treatment access, and program intensity**, while study design limitations make it difficult to separate true causal effects from confounding [N1-F1][N3-R2][N3-R3][N4-F3]. In practice, supported accommodation should be viewed as part of a **reentry system** that includes parole/release decisions, supervision, and behavioral health support, rather than as a standalone magic bullet [N4-F3][N6-R5].
